prompt: Which definition of leakage does the lesson use?
hint: It is about the moment the model is used.

choices.text: Any column with missing values
choices.why: Gaps are a nuisance, not a leak; `rating_90d` has gaps and is legitimate.

choices.text: Training information absent at prediction time
choices.why: Yes. The test is the moment of prediction.

choices.text: Personal data that reached people who should not see it
choices.why: That is a data breach, a different and serious problem.

choices.text: A model that is overfitted to its own training rows
choices.why: Overfitting is caught by validation; leakage passes it.

prompt: Why does an honest-looking validation score not catch a leaking column?
hint: Where do the training and validation rows come from?

choices.text: Validation only measures accuracy, never value
choices.why: Validation can use any score, and every one of them is fooled the same way.

choices.text: Validation rows are always too few to show it
choices.why: Even thousands of validation rows carry the same leak.

choices.text: The model hides the column from the validation rows
choices.why: Models hide nothing; they use whatever they are given.

choices.text: Both sides of the split carry it equally
choices.why: Yes. A leak is a difference between the data and the world, not between the two halves.

prompt: Match each way in to its example in this course.
hint: One of them has no column at all.

pairs.right: A subscriber's rows on both sides

prompt: On the first of the month, when the credit is sent, what does `cancel_reason` hold for each subscriber?
hint: When is it written?

choices.text: Last month's reason
choices.why: Nobody gives a reason without cancelling.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Yes. It is filled in when they cancel, after the snapshot.

choices.text: The reason each subscriber is most likely to give
choices.why: It is not a prediction; it is what a leaver wrote on the form.

choices.text: `price` for everybody
choices.why: Empty for everybody who has not cancelled.

prompt: Which columns are the target in disguise? Choose all that apply.
hint: Is the column written because of the outcome?

choices.text: *Age*, in the churn model
choices.why: Known at the snapshot and not caused by the outcome.

choices.text: *Skips in the last 90 days*, in the churn model
choices.why: Counted before the snapshot, from the history; legitimate.

choices.text: *Number of follow-up calls*, in a model of which leads will close
choices.why: Yes. Promising leads get more calls because they are promising.

choices.text: *Sent to collections*, in a model of who will default
choices.why: Yes. Collections react to the default.

choices.text: *Refund issued*, in a model of who will complain
choices.why: Yes. The refund follows the complaint.

prompt: What should Ana do with `cancel_reason` once she knows it leaks?
hint: It is in the wrong question, not the wrong file.

choices.text: Delete it from every copy of the data, so nobody uses it by mistake again
choices.why: It answers why people left, which is worth knowing.

choices.text: Keep it in the model, but only on a split by time
choices.why: It is perfect on any split and empty in use.

choices.text: Keep it out of the model and use it to study why people left
choices.why: Yes. A leaking column is a column in the wrong question.

choices.text: Fill its gaps with the most common reason
choices.why: That still marks every leaver differently from everybody else.

prompt: What makes `days_since_last_order` leak?
hint: Ask when it was computed.

choices.text: It counts from the export date, not the snapshot
choices.why: Yes. For an old leaver, it measures days after they left.

choices.text: It has too many distinct values
choices.why: Many distinct values is not a leak.

choices.text: Long gaps between orders never predict cancelling
choices.why: Computed as of the snapshot, it would be a fair and useful feature.

choices.text: It is a number, and only categories can leak into a model
choices.why: Any type of column can carry the future.

prompt: In `subtle.py`, the median for leavers falls from 493 days in 2024Q3 to 40 in 2025Q4. By how many days does it fall?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: With the leaking column, the model scores AUC 0.958 on a random split and 0.500 by time. Why did the time split expose it here?
hint: Look at how the leavers' values change across the quarters.

choices.text: The leavers' values shrink towards the export date, so the pattern learned from old months fails on recent ones
choices.why: Yes. A leak that did not drift with the date would have passed.

choices.text: Time splits catch every leak
choices.why: Only leaks whose distortion changes with the date; that was luck here.

choices.text: The time split has fewer leavers
choices.why: It has a similar share; the values are what changed.

choices.text: AUC cannot be computed on time splits
choices.why: It can, and 0.500 is that computation.

prompt: 2,000 columns of random numbers give 68.8% accuracy when the 20 best are chosen before the split. Where does the skill come from?
hint: Which rows were used to pick the columns?

choices.text: 400 rows is enough to learn anything
choices.why: There is nothing to learn in random numbers, however many rows.

choices.text: Logistic regression always beats a coin
choices.why: On noise it cannot, as the honest run shows.

choices.text: Random numbers carry a little signal
choices.why: Done inside each fold, the same columns give 44.5%: no signal.

choices.text: The validation rows helped pick them
choices.why: Yes. They line up with the target there by chance, and the model is rewarded for it.

prompt: With the columns picked inside each fold, what accuracy did `noise.py` report, as a percentage with one decimal place?
hint: The second line of results.

prompt: The general cure is to put every step that learns anything inside the ___, so cross-validation fits it on the training folds only.
hint: `make_pipeline` builds one.

prompt: Why does the lesson call lesson 3's random-split numbers leaks?
hint: Use the definition.

choices.text: A random split always produces a worse model
choices.why: It produces a better-looking score, which is the problem.

choices.text: They were measured on too few rows to be trusted
choices.why: Tens of thousands of rows; the size was not the issue.

choices.text: They used the wrong library
choices.why: The library was the same; the split was the issue.

choices.text: They feed training what use will lack
choices.why: Yes. Through the split rather than through a column.

prompt: A random split approves a new column and a split by time refuses it. Which do you believe, and why?
hint: Which one resembles the day the model is used?

choices.text: Neither; average the two
choices.why: Averaging an honest score with a leaking one gives a leaking one.

choices.text: The random split, because it uses more of the data
choices.why: Using more data is no help if the data includes the future.

choices.text: The split by time
choices.why: Yes. It is the situation the model will be in; in section 04 it was right.

choices.text: The random split, because random means unbiased
choices.why: Random rows from a world that includes the future are an unbiased sample of the wrong world.

prompt: Which of these are symptoms worth stopping for? Choose all that apply.
hint: None of them is proof.

choices.text: An AUC of 0.99 for predicting who cancels a vegetable box
choices.why: Yes. Behaviour is noisier than that.

choices.text: A column whose relation to the target shifts steadily with the snapshot date
choices.why: Yes. It is often measured from a fixed date, like the export.

choices.text: A cross-validation score close to the score on the test months
choices.why: Agreement is reassuring, not suspicious.

choices.text: Dropping one column moves the score far more than dropping any other
choices.why: Yes. That column deserves an interview.

prompt: In `suspects.py` the leak tops the list by one point, just ahead of `rating_90d`. What does that show?
hint: Could the numbers alone tell the two apart?

choices.text: `rating_90d` leaks as well
choices.why: It is averaged from reviews before the snapshot: legitimate.

choices.text: The check is broken
choices.why: It works; it finds blatant leaks and cannot find subtle ones.

choices.text: A subtle leak looks like a good feature, so only asking where it comes from tells them apart
choices.why: Yes. The audit of section 08 is the proof, not the ranking.

choices.text: The leak is too small to matter
choices.why: It more than doubled the model's apparent value.

prompt: A `segment` column says *loyal* for every row of a customer, from 2024 to 2026, though they cancelled twice. Which audit question finds it?
hint: The value never changes across years.

choices.text: Who writes it, and in response to what?
choices.why: Useful, but the tell here is that the value never moves.

choices.text: Will it be there in real time?
choices.why: Availability is a different question from whether its history is true.

choices.text: If it is a summary, over what window?
choices.why: It is a label, not a summary over a window.

choices.text: Does it change after it is first written?
choices.why: Yes. An updated-in-place field holds today's value in every historical row.

prompt: Why can the *as of the snapshot?* column of the audit table not be filled in from the data alone?
hint: `days_since_last_order` looked like a good feature.

choices.text: It is a fact about the systems
choices.why: Yes. It takes asking the owners or reading the code that builds the file.

choices.text: Because pandas cannot read dates
choices.why: It reads them, and dates do not answer this question anyway.

choices.text: Because the table is only for categorical columns
choices.why: Every column gets a line.

choices.text: Because the data has too many rows to inspect by hand
choices.why: Size is not the obstacle; the information is not in the rows.

prompt: Put the anti-leak procedure in order.
hint: The split comes before anything learns.
items: Fill in the audit table for every column
Fit every learned step inside a pipeline
Treat any too-good score as a bug

prompt: A hospital model predicts sepsis at admission. Its strongest column is *antibiotics prescribed in the first 24 hours*. What do you conclude?
hint: Is it known at admission, and why is it written?

choices.text: It should be kept, but scaled before the split so that nothing it learns can reach the validation rows
choices.why: Scaling has nothing to do with it; the column must go.

choices.text: It leaks only if the split is random
choices.why: It leaks on any split; at admission it does not exist.

choices.text: It is a strong, legitimate predictor
choices.why: It is written later than admission, by doctors reacting to suspected sepsis.

choices.text: It leaks twice, from the future and as the target
choices.why: Yes: from the future, and as the target in disguise.
